entities.name: Pierre d'Ailly
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pierre d'Ailly (c. 1351 – August 18, 1420) was a towering intellectual figure of the late medieval era, a French theologian, philosopher, astronomer, astrologer, and cardinal whose career spanned the tumultuous period of the Western Schism. Born in Compiègne, he rose through the ranks of the University of Paris, becoming Chancellor in 1389, and later served as Bishop of Cambrai before his elevation to cardinal by Antipope John XXIII. His profound influence lay in his attempts to reconcile theological orthodoxy with burgeoning scientific inquiry and his prominent, yet often controversial, role in addressing the schism that divided the Roman Catholic Church for four decades. He was a key proponent of conciliarism, arguing for the supremacy of a general council over a pope in times of crisis, a doctrine that profoundly shaped the Council of Constance.

D'Ailly's intellectual output was prodigious, encompassing over 170 known works. As a leading scholar at the University of Paris, he engaged with debates on nominalism and realism, and his *Imago Mundi* (Image of the World), completed around 1410, was a comprehensive cosmographical treatise that synthesized ancient Greek, Islamic, and medieval Christian geographical knowledge. This work, notably read and annotated by Christopher Columbus, underestimated the circumference of the Earth, suggesting a shorter route to the East by sailing west. Furthermore, d'Ailly was instrumental in the efforts to end the Western Schism, participating actively in the Councils of Pisa (1409) and Constance (1414-1418). At Constance, he was a leading voice for conciliar reform, advocating for the deposition of rival popes and the election of a new, universally recognized pontiff, ultimately contributing to the election of Martin V in 1417.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pierre d'Ailly was pivotal in resolving the Western Schism through his conciliarist advocacy at the Council of Constance and his *Imago Mundi* significantly, albeit indirectly, influenced Christopher Columbus's voyages of discovery.
